 $

(\mathcal{W}_1) & \mathcal{W}_{x}\circ y\rightarrow y & (x\not\equiv y)\\

definition.raw:
\label{pervoe} The symbols $x,y,z,\ldots$ are \emph{variables}. The symbols $M,N,L$ range over \emph{terms},
$s,q,r$  range over \emph{substitutions}, and $a,b,c$  range
over variables (they are \emph{metavariables}). The sets of terms
and substitutions are defined inductively as follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= a \mid  MN \mid \lambda a. M \mid s\circ M\\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W}_{a} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ a \rangle \mid
s\circ q
\end{align*}
Note that\\[5pt]
 $\begin{array}{llll}
 s\circ M & \text{corresponds to} & M[s] &\text{ from ~\cite{Abadi}};\\
 s\circ q & \text{corresponds to} & q\circ s &\text{ from ~\cite{Abadi}};\\
\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle & \text{corresponds to} & N\cdot s &\text{ from ~\cite{Abadi}};\\
\mathcal{W}_{a} & \text{corresponds to} & \uparrow &\text{ from
~\cite{Abadi}}.
   \end{array}$\\
definition.clean: The symbols x,y,z,ldots are variables. The symbols M,N,L range over terms, s,q,r range over substitutions, and a,b,c range over variables (they are metavariables). The sets of terms and substitutions are defined inductively as follows: M,N::&= a mid MN mid lambda a. M mid scirc M\\ s,q::&= id mid W_a mid langle s\,,\, N/ a rangle mid scirc q Note that\\[5pt] llll scirc M & corresponds to & M[s] & from ;\\ scirc q & corresponds to & qcirc s & from ;\\ langle s\,,\, N/ arangle & corresponds to & Ncdot s & from ;\\ W_a & corresponds to & uparrow & from . \\

definition.raw:
A \emph{context} is a possibly empty, finite list of variables
with multiplicity (i.e., repetitions are permitted). The symbols
$\Gamma,\Delta,\Sigma,\Psi$ range over contexts.

or of the form $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$.

The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction
sequence $U\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}V$. \\[5pt]
Case 1: If this length is equal to $0$, take any
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Gamma\vdash M$ as $\Sigma\vdash
L$ and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}.
\\[5pt]
 Case 2: Suppose this sequence has the form
 $U\rightarrow \ldots\rightarrow W\rightarrow V$ and
   the sequence
 $U\rightarrow \ldots\rightarrow W$ satisfies the statement of the theorem, i.e.:\\
 $\Gamma\vdash M
\overset{\lambda\mathcal{W}}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Delta\vdash N$ for some $\Delta\vdash
N$, where $\Delta\vdash N$  is
 a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form  and $(\Delta\vdash
N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(W)$.\\[3pt]
 If the reduction step $W\rightarrow
V$ belongs to  $\sigma$, everything is all right,
 because
$\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case and we can use
$\Delta\vdash N$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$.
\\[3pt] If
$W\rightarrow_{Beta}V$, then $\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}. If $\sigma(W)$ coincides with
$\sigma(V)$, everything is all right. Otherwise, suppose
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ has the form
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow_{Beta}W'\overset{\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}\sigma(V)$.
 Any  $Beta$-redex in
$\sigma(W)$
corresponds to some $Beta$-redex in $N$. Contracting this redex in $N$, we obtain\\
$\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{Beta}\Delta\vdash N'$ and $(\Delta\vdash
N')\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W'$, for some $N'$. Take  any
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta\vdash N'$ as
$\Sigma\vdash L$, then use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to obtain\\
$(\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V)$.

proof.raw:
Suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$ M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow M_n\rightarrow\ldots$$
 I claim that we can get
some
infinite  $R$-sequence\\
$$(M_1)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_2)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_n)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots$$
The proof is by induction over $n$. If $n$ is equal to $1$, there is nothing to prove. Else there are three cases.\\[5pt]
1)  If the reduction step $ M_n\rightarrow M_{n+1}$ is not
$Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\\ $R$-reduction of the
same name $(M_n)^*\rightarrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several
$\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2$ can
decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some
black lambda, this lambda may
turn pale. See Example~\ref{example1.18}.\\[5pt]
2) If  $M_n\rightarrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$,
we can apply $\alpha$:\\
$(M_n)^*\rightarrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~\ref{restriction}
and
Example~\ref{example1.13}).\\[5pt]
3) If $ M_n\rightarrow_{Abs} M_{n+1}$ and the $Abs$-redex is
$s\circ\lambda a.M$, there are four
possible subcases:\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
Subcase \,1. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin
FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 2. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 3. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase \,4. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);
\end{array}\\[3pt]
$ and we can apply $Abs_1, Abs_2, Abs_3$, and $Abs_4$,
respectively. See Examples~\ref{example1.14}, \ref{example1.15},
\ref{example1.16}, and \ref{example1.17}.

The proof is similar for substitutions. For judgements, suppose we
have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\Gamma_1\vdash M_1\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_2\vdash  M_2\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_3\vdash M_3\rightsquigarrow\ldots$$
We can obtain the $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence of terms
$$\Lambda\Gamma_1.M_1\arrow\arrow\Lambda\Gamma_2.M_2\arrow\arrow\Lambda\Gamma_3.M_3\arrow\arrow\ldots$$
where $\alpha_2$-steps are replaced by $\alpha_1$ and $Abs$.

For any infinite $R$-sequence
$$M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow M_3\rightarrow\ldots$$
we can get some infinite $Q$-sequence simply by labelling all
symbols $\circ$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda} a$ by theirs own
values. See~\cite{Zantema}, Theorem~81 for details (see
also~\cite{Zantema}, Example~33). The proof  is similar for
substitutions.

\begin{array}{ll} & M[s][q]\rightarrow M[s\circ q]
\end{array}$\\[3pt]
will now look like this\\
$\begin{array}{ll} & [q][s]M\rightarrow[q\circ s]M
\end{array}$\\
Now we can write far fewer parentheses. For example, $[s]\lambda
x.[q]\lambda y.M$ is uniquely deciphered as $[s](\lambda
x.([q](\lambda y.M)))$. I chose the notation $s\circ M$  instead of
$[s]M$, because $s\circ\lambda x.q\circ\lambda y.M$ is easy to read,
this notation is close to the notation of category theory, and we
can now use angle brackets to denote  ordered pairs and nothing
else ($id\circ M$ looks better than $\langle id \rangle M$).\\ After some
doubts I have replaced the symbol $\uparrow$ by $\mathcal{W}$. We will
have to supply this symbol with a subscript, and
$\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\mathcal{W}_y\,,\,\mathcal{W}_z\circ z/ z\rangle$ is much easier to read
than $\langle\uparrow_x\circ\uparrow_y\,,\,\uparrow_z\circ z/ z\rangle$. The
symbols $\mathcal{W}_x$  correspond to $\mathcal{W}_x$ from~\cite{Kesner}
to some extent, but are not the same.

 The sets of untyped
terms and substitutions  are defined inductively as follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= x \mid  MN \mid \lambda x. M \mid s\circ M \\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ x \rangle \mid s\circ q
\end{align*}
where the symbol $x$ denotes an arbitrary variable.

 The sets of typed
terms and substitutions are defined inductively as follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= x \mid  MN \mid \lambda x^A. M \mid s\circ M \\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ x \rangle \mid s\circ q
\end{align*}
where $A$ is an arbitrary type.\\
A usual simultaneous substitution $$[x_1/N_1\,,\,
x_2/N_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, x_k/N_k]$$ in the new notation looks like
$$\langle\ldots\langle\langle id\,,\, N_1/ x_1\rangle\,,\, N_2/ x_2\rangle\,,\,\ldots
N_k/ x_k\rangle$$ For brevity, we will write  $$\langle id\,,\, N_1/
x_1\,,\, N_2/ x_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, N_k/ x_k\rangle$$ But now any two (or
more) of the variables $x_1,\ldots,x_k$
 may
coincide (as in contexts).

A \emph{judgement} is an expression of the form $\Gamma\vdash M:A$
or of the form $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$, where $\Gamma$ and
$\Delta$ are contexts, $A$ is a type, $M$ is a term, and $s$ is a
substitution.
\begin{definition} (Typing rules).\label{type}\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
(i)& \Gamma,x:A\vdash x:A &\\[5pt]
(ii)& \ruleone{\Gamma\vdash
x:A}{\Gamma,y:B\vdash x:A} & (x\not\equiv y) \\[15pt]
(iii)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash M:A\rightarrow B}{\Gamma\vdash
N:A}{\Gamma\vdash
MN:B} &\\[15pt]
(iv)& \ruleone{\Gamma,x:A\vdash M:B}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda x^A.M:A\rightarrow B} &\\[15pt]
(v)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta}{\Delta\vdash
M:A}{\Gamma\vdash
 s\circ M:A} &\\[15pt]
(vi)& \Gamma\vdash id\triangleright\Gamma &\\[5pt]
(vii)& \Gamma,x:A\vdash\mathcal{W} \triangleright\Gamma &\\[5pt]
(viii)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta}{\Gamma\vdash
N:A}{\Gamma\vdash
\langle s\,,\, N/ x\rangle\triangleright\Delta\, ,x:A} &\\[15pt]
(ix)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta}{\Delta\vdash
q\triangleright\Sigma}{\Gamma\vdash s\circ q\triangleright\Sigma} &
\end{array}
$\\[5pt]
\end{definition}
The restriction in the rule $(ii)$ is necessary  because
$\Gamma\vdash x:A$ means ``the rightmost occurrences of the
variable $x$ in the context $\Gamma$ has type $A$."

\begin{example}
$$
\ruleone{x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash x:B}{x:A\,,\, x:B\,,\, y:C\vdash x:B}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruletwo{x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\triangleright x:A}{x:A\vdash x:A}{x:A\,,\,
x:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\circ x:A}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruletwo{\ruletwo{x:A, x:B, y:C\vdash \mathcal{W}\triangleright x:A,x:B}{x:A,
x:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\triangleright x:A}{x:A, x:B, y:C\vdash\mathcal{W}\circ\mathcal{W}\triangleright
x:A}}{x:A\vdash x:A}{x:A, x:B, y:C\vdash (\mathcal{W}\circ\mathcal{W})\circ x:A}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruleone{\ruleone{x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash x:B}{x:A\vdash\lambda
x^B.x:B\rightarrow B}}{\vdash\lambda x^A.\lambda x^B.x:A\rightarrow(B\rightarrow
B)}
$$
\end{example}

 There are no weakening rules except the
rule $(ii)$. But now we have an explicit weakening. For example,
we can derive $\Gamma,y:B\vdash\mathcal{W}\circ M:A$ from  $\Gamma\vdash
M:A$
\begin{example}
$$\ruletwo{\Gamma,y:B\vdash\mathcal{W}\triangleright\Gamma}{\ruledot{ \rule{5mm}{0mm} \Gamma\vdash M:A}}{\Gamma,y:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\circ M:A}$$
\end{example}
If the variable $y$ does not occur in the context $\Gamma$, then
$\mathcal{W}\circ M$ reduces to $M$ in some sense (more precisely,
$\mathcal{W}\circ M$ and $M$ have a common reduct).

The typing rules~\ref{type} have a pleasant property: every
derivable judgement has a unique derivation. This is not true for
the usual typing rules because of weakening rules. This pleasant
property allows us to  determine uniquely the value of any
judgement in some cartesian closed category by induction over the
derivation. Assume that some objects are assigned to types. To
each context of the form
$$x_1:A_1 \,,\, x_2:A_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, x_n:A_n$$
we assign the object
$$(\ldots(\mathbf{1}\times A_1)\times A_2)\times\cdots)\times
A_n)$$ where $\mathbf{1}$ is the (canonical) terminal object.\\
Denote by $A\overset{f\,\circ\, g}{\rightarrow} C$ the composition of
$A\overset{f}{\rightarrow}B$ and
$B\overset{g}{\rightarrow}C$.\\
 To any derivable judgement of the form
$\Gamma\vdash M:A$ we put in correspondence some arrow from
$\Gamma$ to $A$.\\
 To any derivable judgement of the form
$\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$ we put in correspondence some arrow
from $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$.
\begin{definition}
 $(\Gamma\vdash
M:A)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow} A$
  is shorthand for  ``the arrow $\Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow} A$ corresponds to the judgement $\Gamma\vdash
  M:A$."\\
   $(\Gamma\vdash
s\triangleright\Delta)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} \Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow}
\Delta$ is shorthand for ``the arrow $\Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow}
\Delta$ corresponds to the judgement $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$."
\end{definition}

will now look like this\\
$\begin{array}{ll} & [q][s]M\rightarrow[q\circ s]M
\end{array}$\\
Now we can write far fewer parentheses. For example, $[s]\lambda
x.[q]\lambda y.M$ is uniquely deciphered as $[s](\lambda
x.([q](\lambda y.M)))$. I chose the notation $s\circ M$  instead of
$[s]M$, because $s\circ\lambda x.q\circ\lambda y.M$ is easy to read,
this notation is close to the notation of category theory, and we
can now use angle brackets to denote  ordered pairs and nothing
else ($id\circ M$ looks better than $\langle id \rangle M$).\\ After some
doubts I have replaced the symbol $\uparrow$ by $\mathcal{W}$. We will
have to supply this symbol with a subscript, and
$\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\mathcal{W}_y\,,\,\mathcal{W}_z\circ z/ z\rangle$ is much easier to read
than $\langle\uparrow_x\circ\uparrow_y\,,\,\uparrow_z\circ z/ z\rangle$. The
symbols $\mathcal{W}_x$  correspond to $\mathcal{W}_x$ from~\cite{Kesner}
to some extent, but are not the same.

 The sets of untyped
terms and substitutions  are defined inductively as follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= x \mid  MN \mid \lambda x. M \mid s\circ M \\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ x \rangle \mid s\circ q
\end{align*}
where the symbol $x$ denotes an arbitrary variable.

 The sets of typed
terms and substitutions are defined inductively as follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= x \mid  MN \mid \lambda x^A. M \mid s\circ M \\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ x \rangle \mid s\circ q
\end{align*}
where $A$ is an arbitrary type.\\
A usual simultaneous substitution $$[x_1/N_1\,,\,
x_2/N_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, x_k/N_k]$$ in the new notation looks like
$$\langle\ldots\langle\langle id\,,\, N_1/ x_1\rangle\,,\, N_2/ x_2\rangle\,,\,\ldots
N_k/ x_k\rangle$$ For brevity, we will write  $$\langle id\,,\, N_1/
x_1\,,\, N_2/ x_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, N_k/ x_k\rangle$$ But now any two (or
more) of the variables $x_1,\ldots,x_k$
 may
coincide (as in contexts).

A \emph{judgement} is an expression of the form $\Gamma\vdash M:A$
or of the form $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$, where $\Gamma$ and
$\Delta$ are contexts, $A$ is a type, $M$ is a term, and $s$ is a
substitution.
\begin{definition} (Typing rules).\label{type}\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
(i)& \Gamma,x:A\vdash x:A &\\[5pt]
(ii)& \ruleone{\Gamma\vdash
x:A}{\Gamma,y:B\vdash x:A} & (x\not\equiv y) \\[15pt]
(iii)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash M:A\rightarrow B}{\Gamma\vdash
N:A}{\Gamma\vdash
MN:B} &\\[15pt]
(iv)& \ruleone{\Gamma,x:A\vdash M:B}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda x^A.M:A\rightarrow B} &\\[15pt]
(v)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta}{\Delta\vdash
M:A}{\Gamma\vdash
 s\circ M:A} &\\[15pt]
(vi)& \Gamma\vdash id\triangleright\Gamma &\\[5pt]
(vii)& \Gamma,x:A\vdash\mathcal{W} \triangleright\Gamma &\\[5pt]
(viii)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta}{\Gamma\vdash
N:A}{\Gamma\vdash
\langle s\,,\, N/ x\rangle\triangleright\Delta\, ,x:A} &\\[15pt]
(ix)& \ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta}{\Delta\vdash
q\triangleright\Sigma}{\Gamma\vdash s\circ q\triangleright\Sigma} &
\end{array}
$\\[5pt]
\end{definition}
The restriction in the rule $(ii)$ is necessary  because
$\Gamma\vdash x:A$ means ``the rightmost occurrences of the
variable $x$ in the context $\Gamma$ has type $A$."

\begin{example}
$$
\ruleone{x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash x:B}{x:A\,,\, x:B\,,\, y:C\vdash x:B}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruletwo{x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\triangleright x:A}{x:A\vdash x:A}{x:A\,,\,
x:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\circ x:A}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruletwo{\ruletwo{x:A, x:B, y:C\vdash \mathcal{W}\triangleright x:A,x:B}{x:A,
x:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\triangleright x:A}{x:A, x:B, y:C\vdash\mathcal{W}\circ\mathcal{W}\triangleright
x:A}}{x:A\vdash x:A}{x:A, x:B, y:C\vdash (\mathcal{W}\circ\mathcal{W})\circ x:A}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruleone{\ruleone{x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash x:B}{x:A\vdash\lambda
x^B.x:B\rightarrow B}}{\vdash\lambda x^A.\lambda x^B.x:A\rightarrow(B\rightarrow
B)}
$$
\end{example}

 There are no weakening rules except the
rule $(ii)$. But now we have an explicit weakening. For example,
we can derive $\Gamma,y:B\vdash\mathcal{W}\circ M:A$ from  $\Gamma\vdash
M:A$
\begin{example}
$$\ruletwo{\Gamma,y:B\vdash\mathcal{W}\triangleright\Gamma}{\ruledot{ \rule{5mm}{0mm} \Gamma\vdash M:A}}{\Gamma,y:B\vdash \mathcal{W}\circ M:A}$$
\end{example}
If the variable $y$ does not occur in the context $\Gamma$, then
$\mathcal{W}\circ M$ reduces to $M$ in some sense (more precisely,
$\mathcal{W}\circ M$ and $M$ have a common reduct).

The typing rules~\ref{type} have a pleasant property: every
derivable judgement has a unique derivation. This is not true for
the usual typing rules because of weakening rules. This pleasant
property allows us to  determine uniquely the value of any
judgement in some cartesian closed category by induction over the
derivation. Assume that some objects are assigned to types. To
each context of the form
$$x_1:A_1 \,,\, x_2:A_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, x_n:A_n$$
we assign the object
$$(\ldots(\mathbf{1}\times A_1)\times A_2)\times\cdots)\times
A_n)$$ where $\mathbf{1}$ is the (canonical) terminal object.\\
Denote by $A\overset{f\,\circ\, g}{\rightarrow} C$ the composition of
$A\overset{f}{\rightarrow}B$ and
$B\overset{g}{\rightarrow}C$.\\
 To any derivable judgement of the form
$\Gamma\vdash M:A$ we put in correspondence some arrow from
$\Gamma$ to $A$.\\
 To any derivable judgement of the form
$\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$ we put in correspondence some arrow
from $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$.
\begin{definition}
 $(\Gamma\vdash
M:A)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow} A$
  is shorthand for  ``the arrow $\Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow} A$ corresponds to the judgement $\Gamma\vdash
  M:A$."\\
   $(\Gamma\vdash
s\triangleright\Delta)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} \Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow}
\Delta$ is shorthand for ``the arrow $\Gamma\overset{f}{\rightarrow}
\Delta$ corresponds to the judgement $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$."
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}A term $M$ is called \emph{pure} iff it does not
contain sub-terms of the shape $s\circ N$.
\end{definition}
\begin{theorem}
If $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable and $\Gamma\vdash M$ is a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form (with respect to $\rightsquigarrow$), then $M$ is
pure.\label{pure}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $M$ contain a sub-term of the shape $s\circ N$; then $N$
must be a variable (we  denote it by $b$), else we can apply
$Abs, App$ or $Clos$. The substitution $s$ is a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form  and must have the form
$\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_n}$ (see theorem~\ref{Subnf}), else we can
apply $IdVar, ConsVar$ or $New$. Further,  $a_n$ in
$(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_n})\circ b$ must coincide with $b$, else we
can apply $\mathcal{W}_1$ or $\mathcal{W}_2$. We see that $M$ must be constructed
from  variables and  blocks of the form
 $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b\quad (m\geqslant 0)$ by
using application and abstraction. To conclude the proof, it is
sufficient to prove the following lemma.
\end{proof}
\begin{lemma}
If $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable and $M$ is constructed from
variables and  blocks of the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ
b\quad(m\geqslant 0)$ by using application and abstraction, then
$M$ is pure (this means that $M$ does not contain blocks) or we
can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash M$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}The proof is by induction over the structure of $M$. Let us consider four cases.\\[5pt]
Case 1: $M$ is a variable. The proof is trivial.\\[5pt]
 Case 2:  $ M$
has the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. By Generation
lemma, $\Gamma\vdash M$
has the form\\
$\Delta\,,\,b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\, a_1\vdash
(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$  \\
and we can apply $\alpha_2$ , because\\
 $FV(b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\,
a_1\vdash (\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b)=\langle\{b\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle$\\[10pt]
 Case 3: $M$ has the form $\lambda a.N$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma,a\vdash
N$ is derivable. Suppose $N$ contains a block of the form
 $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. By
induction hypothesis, we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to
$\Gamma,a\vdash N$. But any application  of $\alpha_1$ or
$\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma,a\vdash N$ corresponds to some application
of $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ (and, in some cases, $Abs$) to
$\Gamma\vdash\lambda a.N$. For example,\\
$\Gamma,a\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_2}\Gamma,b \vdash\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ N$\\
corresponds to\\
 $\Gamma\vdash\lambda
a.N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_1}\Gamma\vdash\lambda b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ N$\\[10pt]
 Case 4: $M$ has the form $NL$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma\vdash N$ and
$\Gamma\vdash L$ are derivable. Suppose one of these terms
contains a block of the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. For
clarity, let it be $N$. By induction hypothesis,  we can apply
$\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash N$. I claim that we can
apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash NL$. For the case
$\alpha_1$ is nothing to prove, because any $\alpha_1$-redex in
$N$ occurs in $NL$ too. For the case $\alpha_2$, suppose that
$\Gamma\vdash NL$ has the form $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$. Recall
that $FV(NL)=FV(N)\cup FV(L)$, hence $FV(N)\subseteq FV(NL)$. By
Lemma~\ref{monotone},\\ $FV(a,\Delta\vdash N))\subseteq FV(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$.\\
Hence if $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash N)$,
then $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$. If
we can apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash N$, then we can
apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$.
\end{proof}

and the substitution\\ $\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ y\rangle$\\ is a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form.

Recall that $O_s$ is also monotone   with respect to $\subseteq$
for any $s$.
\begin{lemma}\label{subfreevar}
If $M_1\rightarrow M_2$, then $FV(M_2)\sqsubseteq FV(M_1)$. If
$s_1\rightarrow s_2$, then $O_{s_2}(\mathcal{A})\sqsubseteq
O_{s_1}(\mathcal{A})$ for any $\mathcal{A}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}The proof is straightforward, but tedious. For example, consider\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{(Abs)} & s\circ \lambda a.M\rightarrow\lambda a.\langle
\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M &
\end{array}
$\\
$\begin{array}{ll} FV(\lambda a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M) &
\\
=FV(\lambda a.((\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ
s)\circ\lambda a.M)a) & (Lemma~\ref{corollary3})\\
=FV(\lambda a.(\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ
s\circ\lambda a.M)a) & (Lemma~\ref{corollary23})\\
=O_{\lambda a}(O_{\mathcal{W}}(FV
(s\circ\lambda a.M))\bigcup FV(a)) & \\
=O_{\lambda a}(\langle\{a\},FV_1(s\circ\lambda a.M),FV_2(s\circ\lambda
a.M),\ldots\rangle) & \\
=FV(s\circ\lambda a.M) \end{array}$\\
 $\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{(App)} & s\circ MN \rightarrow(s\circ  M)(s\circ  N) &
\end{array}
$\\
 $\begin{array}{l}
FV(s\circ  MN) \\
=O_s(FV(MN))\\
=O_s(FV(M)\cup FV(N))\\
\supseteq
O_s(FV(M))\cup O_s(FV(N))\\
=FV(s\circ M)\cup FV(s\circ N)\\
=FV((s\circ M)(s\circ N)) \end{array}$\\
 $
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{(ConsVar)} & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ a\rightarrow
N &
\end{array}
$\\
$\begin{array}{l}
 FV(\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ a)\\
 =O_{\langle
s\,,\, N/ a\rangle}(FV(a))\\
=O_s(O_{\lambda a}(FV(a)))\cup FV(N)\\
\supseteq
FV(N)
\end{array}$\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{(New)} & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ b\rightarrow s\circ
b & (a\neq b)
\end{array}
$\\
$\begin{array}{l} FV(\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ
b)\\
=O_{\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle}(FV(b))\\
=O_s(O_{\lambda a}(FV(b)))\cup FV(N)\\
\supseteq O_s(O_{\lambda a}(FV(b)))\\
=O_s(O_{\lambda
a}(\langle\{b\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)\\
=O_s(\langle\{b\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)\\
=O_s(FV(b))\\
=FV(s\circ b)
\end{array}$\\ 
$\begin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(ConsShift)} & \langle s\,,\, N/
a\rangle\circ \mathcal{W}_{a}\rightarrow s &
\end{array}
$\\
$\begin{array}{l} O_{\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ
\mathcal{W}_{a}}(\mathcal{A})\\

\supseteq O_s(O_{\lambda
a}(O_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{A})))\\
=O_s(O_{\lambda
a}(\langle\emptyset,\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\ldots\rangle)\\
=O_s(\langle\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\ldots\rangle)\\
=O_s(\mathcal{A})
\end{array}$\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}

a\rangle\rightarrow\langle s\circ q \,,\, s\circ N/ a\rangle &
\end{array}
$\\

a\rangle}(\mathcal{A})\\

a\rangle}(\mathcal{A}))\\

=O_{s\circ q}(O_{\lambda a}(\mathcal{A}))\cup FV(s\circ
N)\\

N/ a\rangle}(\mathcal{A})
\end{array}$\\
$

b)\\

=O_{\lambda b}(\langle\{b\},FV_1(\lambda a.M),FV_2(\lambda
a.M),\ldots\rangle) & \\
=FV(\lambda a.M)
\end{array} $\\[3pt]
In addition, it is  necessary to prove that all operations from

\end{proof}

 To prove that $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$ is strongly
normalizing, we consider the following two-sorted term rewriting
system $R$.
\begin{definition} The signature of $R$ contains:\\ $
\begin{array}{ll}
M,N,L,\ldots & \text{variables};\\
s,q,r,\ldots & \text{variables};\\
 x,y,z,\ldots & \text{constants};\\
id,\mathcal{W}_x,\mathcal{W}_y,\mathcal{W}_z,\ldots &\text{constants};\\
\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of
arity one};\\
\boldsymbol{\lambda} x,\boldsymbol{\lambda} y,\boldsymbol{\lambda}
z,\ldots
& \text{functional symbols of arity one};\\
\cdot\,,\,\circ & \text{functional symbols of arity two};\\
\langle -\,,\, -/ x\rangle,\langle -\,,\, -/ y\rangle,\langle -\,,\, -/ z\rangle,\ldots &
\text{functional symbols of arity two}.
\end{array}
$ \\[5pt]
 We
will omit $\cdot$, which denotes application. The sets of ground
terms and ground substitutions of $R$ are defined inductively as
follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= a \mid  MN \mid \lambda a. M \mid\boldsymbol{\lambda} a. M\mid s\circ M \\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W}_{a} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ a \rangle \mid
s\circ q
\end{align*}
\end{definition}
 We will use the same abbreviations as in
Convention~\ref{notation2} and Convention~\ref{notation1}.
\newpage
\begin{definition}(The rewriting system $R$).\\[5pt]
$
\begin{array}{lll}
(Abs1) & s\circ \lambda a.M\rightarrow\lambda a.\langle
\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs2) & s\circ \boldsymbol{\lambda}
a.M\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\lambda} a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\,
a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs3) & s\circ \lambda a.M\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\lambda}
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs4) & s\circ \boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M\rightarrow\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(App) & s\circ  MN\rightarrow(s\circ  M)(s\circ  N) &\\
(ConsVar) & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ a\rightarrow N &\\
(New) & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ b\rightarrow  s\circ b & (a\neq b)\\
(IdVar) &  id\circ a\rightarrow a &\\
(Clos) & s\circ q\circ M\rightarrow (s\circ q)\circ M &\\
(Ass) & s\circ q\circ  r\rightarrow (s\circ q)\circ r &\\
(IdR) & s\circ id\rightarrow s &\\
(IdShift) & id\circ \mathcal{W}_{a}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}_{a} &\\
(ConsShift) & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ \mathcal{W}_{a}\rightarrow s &\\
(Map) & s\circ \langle q\,,\, N/ a\rangle\rightarrow\langle

(\mathcal{W}_1) & \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ b\rightarrow b & (a\neq b)\\
(\mathcal{W}_2) & (s\circ\mathcal{W}_{a})\circ b\rightarrow s\circ b & (a \neq
b)\\
(\alpha) & \boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M\rightarrow\lambda
b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\, b/ a\rangle\circ M &\\
(\xi) & \boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M\rightarrow\lambda a.M &
\end{array}
$
\end{definition}
\begin{definition} To each term $M$  we assign
$FV(M)$ as in Definition~\ref{FV} with the additional case: \\
$\begin{array}{l} FV(\boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M)=FV(\lambda
a.M)=O_{\lambda a}(FV(M)) \end{array}$
\end{definition}
\begin{lemma}If $M_1\overset{R}{\rightarrow}M_2$, then $FV(M_2)\sqsubseteq
FV(M_1)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}See Lemma~\ref{subfreevar}.
\end{proof}
\begin{lemma}\label{restriction}The restriction $(*)$ in Definition~\ref{lambdapi} can be
written as\\
$
\begin{array}{ll}
(*) & a \in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda a.M);\quad
b\notin \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ M
 )\\
 \end{array}
$
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}$FV(\lambda b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\, b/
a\rangle\circ M )=FV(\lambda a.M) $ by Lemma~\ref{subfreevar} (the
case $\alpha_1$).
\end{proof}
\begin{definition}By $M^*$ denote the term $M$ in which all sub-terms of
the shape $\lambda a.L$, such that $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant
1}FV_i(\lambda a.L)$, are replaced  by $\boldsymbol{\lambda}
a.L$.
\end{definition}
\begin{theorem}If $R$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions, then $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$ is strongly normalizing (on the sets of terms, substitutions, and judgements of
the form $\Gamma\vdash M$).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}Suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$ M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow M_n\rightarrow\ldots$$
 I claim that we can get
some
infinite  $R$-sequence\\
$$(M_1)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_2)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_n)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots$$
The proof is by induction over $n$. If $n$ is equal to $1$, there is nothing to prove. Else there are three cases.\\[5pt]
1)  If the reduction step $ M_n\rightarrow M_{n+1}$ is not
$Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\\ $R$-reduction of the
same name $(M_n)^*\rightarrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several
$\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2$ can
decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some
black lambda, this lambda may
turn pale. See Example~\ref{example1.18}.\\[5pt]
2) If  $M_n\rightarrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$,
we can apply $\alpha$:\\
$(M_n)^*\rightarrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~\ref{restriction}
and
Example~\ref{example1.13}).\\[5pt]
3) If $ M_n\rightarrow_{Abs} M_{n+1}$ and the $Abs$-redex is
$s\circ\lambda a.M$, there are four
possible subcases:\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
Subcase \,1. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin
FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 2. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 3. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase \,4. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);
\end{array}\\[3pt]
$ and we can apply $Abs_1, Abs_2, Abs_3$, and $Abs_4$,
respectively. See Examples~\ref{example1.14}, \ref{example1.15},
\ref{example1.16}, and \ref{example1.17}.

x.[q]\lambda y.M$ is uniquely deciphered as $[s](\lambda
x.([q](\lambda y.M)))$. I chose the notation $s\circ M$  instead of
$[s]M$, because $s\circ\lambda x.q\circ\lambda y.M$ is easy to read,
this notation is close to the notation of category theory, and we
can now use angle brackets to denote  ordered pairs and nothing
else ($id\circ M$ looks better than $\langle id \rangle M$).\\ After some

have to supply this symbol with a subscript, and

symbols $\mathcal{W}_x$  correspond to $\mathcal{W}_x$ from~\cite{Kesner}
to some extent, but are not the same.

\begin{definition}A \emph{name-free judgement} is an expression of the
form $m\vdash U$ or of the form $m\vdash u$, where $m\in
N,m\geqslant 0$.
\end{definition}
Informally, $m$ is ``the length of an invisible context".

M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$ is shorthand for ``the name-free
judgement $m\vdash U$
 corresponds to the  judgement $\Gamma\vdash M$." \\
$(\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta)\Rightarrow(m\vdash u)$ is shorthand
for ``the
 name-free judgement $m\vdash u$  corresponds to the
judgement $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$."
\end{definition}
\begin{definition}By $|\Gamma|$ denote the length of $\Gamma$.
\end{definition}

$

Now we can write far fewer parentheses. For example, $[s]\lambda
x.[q]\lambda y.M$ is uniquely deciphered as $[s](\lambda
x.([q](\lambda y.M)))$. I chose the notation $s\circ M$  instead of
$[s]M$, because $s\circ\lambda x.q\circ\lambda y.M$ is easy to read,
this notation is close to the notation of category theory, and we
can now use angle brackets to denote  ordered pairs and nothing
else ($id\circ M$ looks better than $\langle id \rangle M$).\\ After some
doubts I have replaced the symbol $\uparrow$ by $\mathcal{W}$. We will
have to supply this symbol with a subscript, and
$\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\mathcal{W}_y\,,\,\mathcal{W}_z\circ z/ z\rangle$ is much easier to read
than $\langle\uparrow_x\circ\uparrow_y\,,\,\uparrow_z\circ z/ z\rangle$. The
symbols $\mathcal{W}_x$  correspond to $\mathcal{W}_x$ from~\cite{Kesner}
to some extent, but are not the same.

It is clear that any pure term is constructed from the symbols
$\underline{n}$ by  using application and  abstraction.
\begin{definition}A \emph{name-free judgement} is an expression of the
form $m\vdash U$ or of the form $m\vdash u$, where $m\in
N,m\geqslant 0$.
\end{definition}
Informally, $m$ is ``the length of an invisible context".
\begin{definition} $(\Gamma\vdash
M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$ is shorthand for ``the name-free
judgement $m\vdash U$
 corresponds to the  judgement $\Gamma\vdash M$." \\
$(\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta)\Rightarrow(m\vdash u)$ is shorthand
for ``the
 name-free judgement $m\vdash u$  corresponds to the
judgement $\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta$."
\end{definition}
\begin{definition}By $|\Gamma|$ denote the length of $\Gamma$.
\end{definition}
\begin{definition}\label{deftransfer}(The rules of correspondence between judgements and name-free judgements).\\
$
\begin{array}{ll}
(i)& (\Gamma,a\vdash a)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma,a|\vdash \underline{1}) \\[5pt]
 (ii)& \ruleone{(\Gamma\vdash
a)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash \underline{n})}{(\Gamma,b\vdash a)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma,b| \vdash \underline{n+1})\using {\quad(a\neq b)}}\\[20pt]
 (iii)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash U)}{(\Gamma\vdash N)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash V)}{(\Gamma\vdash
MN)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma|  \vdash UV)}\\[15pt]
 (iv)& \ruleone{(\Gamma,a\vdash M)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma,a| \vdash U)}{(\Gamma\vdash\lambda a.M)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash \lambda U) }\\[15pt]
 (v)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash s \triangleright\Delta)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash u) }{(\Delta\vdash M)\Rightarrow  (|\Delta| \vdash U)}{(\Gamma\vdash
 s \circ M)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash u \circ U)}\\[15pt]
(vi)& (\Gamma\vdash id \triangleright\Gamma)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash id ) \\[5pt]
(vii)& (\Gamma,a\vdash\mathcal{W}_{a} \triangleright\Gamma)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma,a| \vdash \mathcal{W} ) \\[5pt]
(viii)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash s \triangleright\Delta)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma|
\vdash u ) }{(\Gamma\vdash N)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma| \vdash
V)}{(\Gamma\vdash
\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle \triangleright\Delta ,a)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash\langle u\,,\, V\rangle )}\\[15pt]
(ix)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash s \triangleright\Delta)\Rightarrow  (|\Gamma|
\vdash u) }{(\Delta\vdash q \triangleright\Sigma)\Rightarrow (|\Delta|
\vdash v ) }{(\Gamma \vdash s \circ q \triangleright\Sigma)\Rightarrow
(|\Gamma|
\vdash u \circ v )}\\
\end{array}
$
\end{definition}
\begin{corollary}If $(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$, then
$m=|\Gamma|$.\\
 If $(\Gamma\vdash s\triangleright\Delta)\Rightarrow(m\vdash u)$, then $m=|\Gamma|$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{example}
$$
(x\vdash x)\Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1})
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruleone{(x\vdash x)\Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1})}{(x,y
\vdash x)\Rightarrow (2 \vdash \underline{2})}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}
$$
\ruletwo{(x,y \vdash \mathcal{W}_y\triangleright x) \Rightarrow (2 \vdash \mathcal{W})}{(x
\vdash x) \Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1})}{(x,y \vdash
\mathcal{W}_y\circ x) \Rightarrow
 (2 \vdash \mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})}
$$
\end{example}
\begin{definition}($\alpha$-equivalence).\\
 We say that $\Gamma\vdash M$ is $\alpha$-\emph{equal} to $\Delta\vdash N$  and write\\
$(\Gamma\vdash M)\equiv_{\alpha}(\Delta\vdash N)$ iff\\
$(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow (m\vdash U)$ and\\ $(\Delta\vdash
N)\Rightarrow (m\vdash U)$, for some $m,U$.
\end{definition}
\begin{example}$ $\\
$(x,y\vdash\mathcal{W}_y\circ x)\Rightarrow (2\vdash
\mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})$\\
$(x,x\vdash\mathcal{W}_x\circ x)\Rightarrow (2\vdash
\mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})$\\
 $(x,y\vdash\mathcal{W}_y\circ
x)\equiv_{\alpha} (x,x\vdash\mathcal{W}_x\circ x)$
\end{example}
\begin{example}$ $\\
$(x\vdash\lambda y.\mathcal{W}_y\circ x)\Rightarrow (1\vdash
\lambda\mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})$\\
$(x\vdash\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x)\Rightarrow (1\vdash
\lambda\mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})$\\
 $(x\vdash\lambda y.\mathcal{W}_y\circ
x)\equiv_{\alpha} (x\vdash\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x)$
\end{example}
\begin{example}$ $\\
$(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda y.\mathcal{W}_y\circ x)\Rightarrow (0\vdash
\lambda\lambda\mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})$\\
$(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x)\Rightarrow (0\vdash
\lambda\lambda\mathcal{W}\circ \underline{1})$\\
 $(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda y.\mathcal{W}_y\circ
x)\equiv_{\alpha} (\vdash\lambda x.\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x)$
\end{example}
Warning! We can apply $\mathcal{W}_1$ to the term $\lambda x.\lambda
y.\mathcal{W}_y\circ x$, but not to the term $\lambda x.\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ
x$ (and we can apply $\alpha_1$ to the term $\lambda x.\lambda
x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x$, but not to the term $\lambda x.\lambda y.\mathcal{W}_y\circ
x$).
\begin{example}\label{counterexample}$ $\\
$(x,y\vdash x)
\backsimeq (x,y\vdash\mathcal{W}_y\circ x)$\\
 $(x,y\vdash x)\,{\not\equiv_{\alpha}} (x,y\vdash\mathcal{W}_y\circ x)$
 \end{example}
 \begin{lemma}If $(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$, then
 $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable.
 \end{lemma}
 \begin{proof}The proof is straightforward, see Definition~\ref{defsequentsder} and
 Definition~\ref{deftransfer}.
 \end{proof}
\begin{corollary}If $(\Gamma\vdash M)\equiv_{\alpha}(\Delta\vdash N)$, then $\Gamma\vdash
M$ and $\Delta\vdash N$ are derivable.
\end{corollary}

If $\Gamma\vdash M_1$ is derivable and $M_1\rightarrow M_2$, then
$\Gamma\vdash M_2$ is derivable.\\

\begin{proof}
Suppose $M$ contain a sub-term of the shape $s\circ N$; then $N$
must be a variable (we  denote it by $b$), else we can apply
$Abs, App$ or $Clos$. The substitution $s$ is a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form  and must have the form
$\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_n}$ (see theorem~\ref{Subnf}), else we can
apply $IdVar, ConsVar$ or $New$. Further,  $a_n$ in
$(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_n})\circ b$ must coincide with $b$, else we
can apply $\mathcal{W}_1$ or $\mathcal{W}_2$. We see that $M$ must be constructed
from  variables and  blocks of the form
 $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b\quad (m\geqslant 0)$ by
using application and abstraction. To conclude the proof, it is
sufficient to prove the following lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}The proof is by induction over the structure of $M$. Let us consider four cases.\\[5pt]
Case 1: $M$ is a variable. The proof is trivial.\\[5pt]
 Case 2:  $ M$
has the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. By Generation
lemma, $\Gamma\vdash M$
has the form\\
$\Delta\,,\,b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\, a_1\vdash
(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$  \\
and we can apply $\alpha_2$ , because\\
 $FV(b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\,
a_1\vdash (\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b)=\langle\{b\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle$\\[10pt]
 Case 3: $M$ has the form $\lambda a.N$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma,a\vdash
N$ is derivable. Suppose $N$ contains a block of the form
 $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. By
induction hypothesis, we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to
$\Gamma,a\vdash N$. But any application  of $\alpha_1$ or
$\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma,a\vdash N$ corresponds to some application
of $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ (and, in some cases, $Abs$) to
$\Gamma\vdash\lambda a.N$. For example,\\
$\Gamma,a\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_2}\Gamma,b \vdash\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ N$\\
corresponds to\\
 $\Gamma\vdash\lambda
a.N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_1}\Gamma\vdash\lambda b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ N$\\[10pt]
 Case 4: $M$ has the form $NL$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma\vdash N$ and
$\Gamma\vdash L$ are derivable. Suppose one of these terms
contains a block of the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. For
clarity, let it be $N$. By induction hypothesis,  we can apply
$\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash N$. I claim that we can
apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash NL$. For the case
$\alpha_1$ is nothing to prove, because any $\alpha_1$-redex in
$N$ occurs in $NL$ too. For the case $\alpha_2$, suppose that
$\Gamma\vdash NL$ has the form $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$. Recall
that $FV(NL)=FV(N)\cup FV(L)$, hence $FV(N)\subseteq FV(NL)$. By
Lemma~\ref{monotone},\\ $FV(a,\Delta\vdash N))\subseteq FV(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$.\\
Hence if $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash N)$,
then $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$. If
we can apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash N$, then we can
apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$.
\end{proof}
 Warning!
In general, the terms $N_1,\ldots,N_k$ in the statement of
Theorem~\ref{Subnf} are not pure.  For example, the judgement\\
$x,x\vdash\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ y\rangle\triangleright x,x,y$\\ is derivable
and the substitution\\ $\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ y\rangle$\\ is a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form.
\newpage

\begin{proof}$\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable by
Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Sigma\vdash L$ is derivable by Subject
reduction. Therefore $L$ is pure  and $V$ is a $\sigma$-normal
form (Theorem~\ref{pure}, Lemma~\ref{purelemma}). Why
$U\overset{\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}V$? It is sufficient to prove that
$\sigma(U)\equiv\sigma(V)$ ($U$ reduces to its $\sigma$-normal
form because $\sigma$ is strongly normalizing and confluent). The
proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $
\Gamma\vdash M\overset{\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Sigma\vdash L$. If
this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise,
suppose this sequence has the form
\\
$\Gamma\vdash M\rightsquigarrow\ldots\rightsquigarrow\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,\\
where
 $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W$ and $\sigma(U)\equiv\sigma(W)$.\\
   Any possible $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-reduction  step $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,
except  $New,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2,\alpha_1$, and $\alpha_2$ corresponds to
the same name $\sigma$-reduction step of the  nameless terms
$W\rightarrow V$, hence $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in these cases. For
$\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ use Lemma~\ref{lemmauparrow}.\\
(\textbf{Case} $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}_1}.) \quad \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ b\rightarrow b
\qquad(a\neq b)$
$$\ruletwo{\Gamma,a\vdash
\mathcal{W}_{a}\triangleright\Gamma}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash
b}}{\Gamma,a\vdash\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ b}\qquad
\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash b}}{\Gamma,a\vdash b}$$
Suppose \\
 $(\Gamma\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\
  then\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ
b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\mathcal{W}\circ\underline{n}$ and\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n+1}$.\\
We see that
$\sigma(\mathcal{W}\circ\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(\underline{n+1})$.
\\[5pt]
(\textbf{Case} $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}_2}.) \quad (s\circ\mathcal{W}_{a})\circ
b\rightarrow s\circ b \qquad(a\neq b)$
$$\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash
s\triangleright\Gamma,a}}{\Gamma,a\vdash\mathcal{W}_{a}\triangleright\Gamma}{\Delta\vdash
s\circ\mathcal{W}_{a}\triangleright\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash b}}{\Delta\vdash
(s\circ\mathcal{W}_{a})\circ b}\qquad \ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash
s\triangleright\Gamma,a}}{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash
b}}{\Gamma,a\vdash b}}{\Delta\vdash s\circ b}$$
Suppose \\
$(\Delta\vdash s\triangleright\Gamma,a)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u$;\\
 $(\Gamma\vdash
b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\
then\\
$(\Delta\vdash (s\circ\mathcal{W}_{a})\circ b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} (u\circ\mathcal{W})\circ\underline{n}$;\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} \underline{n+1}$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash s\circ b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u\circ\underline{n+1}$.\\
We see that\\
$\sigma((u\circ\mathcal{W})\circ\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\circ\underline{n+1})$\\[5pt]
(\textbf{Case} ${\mathbf{New}}.) \quad \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ
b\rightarrow s\circ b \qquad(a\neq b)$
$$\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash
s\triangleright\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash N}}{\Delta\vdash\langle s\,,\, N/
a\rangle\triangleright\Gamma,a}}{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash
b}}{\Gamma,a\vdash b}}{\Delta\vdash\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ
b}\qquad \ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash
s\triangleright\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash b}}{\Delta\vdash s\circ b}$$
Suppose \\
$(\Delta\vdash s\triangleright\Gamma)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} V$;\\
$(\Gamma\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\
then\\
$(\Gamma,a\vdash b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n+1}$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash\langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ
b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\langle
u\,,\, V\rangle\circ\underline{n+1}$;\\
$(\Delta\vdash s\circ b)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}
u\circ\underline{n}$.\\
We see that\\
$\sigma(\langle u\,,\, V\rangle\circ\underline{n+1})\equiv\sigma(\langle u\,,\,
V\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}\circ\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\circ\underline{n})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $\Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\mathcal{W}}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Sigma\vdash
L$.  If this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise, suppose this sequence has the form
\\
$\Gamma\vdash M\rightsquigarrow\ldots\rightsquigarrow\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,\\
where
$(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}  W$ and  $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}\sigma(W)$.\\
If the reduction step $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$ belongs to
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$, everything is all right, because
$\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case. Indeed, $\Gamma\vdash M$
is derivable by Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Delta\vdash N$ and
$\Sigma\vdash L$ are derivable by Subject
reduction. Take any $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Sigma\vdash L$ (this normal form exists by Theorem ~\ref{SN} and are derivable too) and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to get $ W\overset{\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}\sigma(V)$.\\
If $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{Beta}\Sigma\vdash L$, then
$W\rightarrow_{Beta}V$, because any $Beta$-redex in $N$ corresponds to
some $Beta$-redex in $W$, hence
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction
sequence $U\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}V$. \\[5pt]
Case 1: If this length is equal to $0$, take any
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Gamma\vdash M$ as $\Sigma\vdash
L$ and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}.
\\[5pt]
 Case 2: Suppose this sequence has the form
 $U\rightarrow \ldots\rightarrow W\rightarrow V$ and
   the sequence
 $U\rightarrow \ldots\rightarrow W$ satisfies the statement of the theorem, i.e.:\\
 $\Gamma\vdash M
\overset{\lambda\mathcal{W}}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Delta\vdash N$ for some $\Delta\vdash
N$, where $\Delta\vdash N$  is
 a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form  and $(\Delta\vdash
N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(W)$.\\[3pt]
 If the reduction step $W\rightarrow
V$ belongs to  $\sigma$, everything is all right,
 because
$\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case and we can use
$\Delta\vdash N$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$.
\\[3pt] If
$W\rightarrow_{Beta}V$, then $\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}. If $\sigma(W)$ coincides with
$\sigma(V)$, everything is all right. Otherwise, suppose
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ has the form
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow_{Beta}W'\overset{\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}\sigma(V)$.
 Any  $Beta$-redex in
$\sigma(W)$
corresponds to some $Beta$-redex in $N$. Contracting this redex in $N$, we obtain\\
$\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{Beta}\Delta\vdash N'$ and $(\Delta\vdash
N')\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W'$, for some $N'$. Take  any
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta\vdash N'$ as
$\Sigma\vdash L$, then use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to obtain\\
$(\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V)$.
\end{proof}
\newpage

 Let $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ be any $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta_1\vdash N_1$ and let $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ be

 $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\equiv_{\alpha}(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.

\begin{proof}By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\backsimeq(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)$.\\ Suppose
$(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$;
$(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$;\\
$(\Delta_1\vdash N_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}V_1$; and
$(\Delta_2\vdash N_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}V_2$.\\
 By
Theorem~\ref{theorem33}, we have
$\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow} \sigma(V_1)$ and
$\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow} \sigma(V_2)$.\\  We know
that $\lambda\sigma$ is confluent, hence
$\sigma(V_1)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow} V$ and
 $\sigma(V_2)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow} V$ for
some $V$. Therefore $V_1\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow} V$ and
$V_2\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow} V$. By Theorem~\ref{theorem44},
we have $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ and
$\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ such that\\
$\begin{array}{l}  \Delta_1\vdash
N_1\overset{\lambda\mathcal{W}}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Sigma_1\vdash
L_1;\\
 \Delta_2\vdash N_2\overset{\lambda\mathcal{W}}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}\Sigma_2\vdash L_2;\\
 \Sigma_1\vdash L_1 \text{ is a $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form};\\
\Sigma_2\vdash L_2 \text{ is a $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form};\\
(\Sigma_1\vdash V_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V);\\
(\Sigma_2\vdash V_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V).
\end{array}$\\[5pt]
Hence  $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\backsimeq(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$. Note
that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are pure (Theorem~\ref{pure}). Note that
$|\Sigma_1|=|\Sigma_2|=|\Gamma_1|=|\Gamma_2|$ (because all
reductions preserve lengths of contexts). By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv},
we have\\
 $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\equiv_{\alpha}(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.
\end{proof}
\begin{definition}By $\Lambda\mathcal{W}$ denote the set of derivable judgements of
the form $\Gamma\vdash M$.

$\overset{\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha}{\rightsquigarrow\rightsquigarrow}$ are confluent (up to $\equiv_{\alpha}$)
on the set $\Lambda\mathcal{W}$.

To prove that $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$ is strongly
normalizing, we consider the following two-sorted term rewriting
system $R$.
\begin{definition} The signature of $R$ contains:\\ $
\begin{array}{ll}
M,N,L,\ldots & \text{variables};\\
s,q,r,\ldots & \text{variables};\\
 x,y,z,\ldots & \text{constants};\\
id,\mathcal{W}_x,\mathcal{W}_y,\mathcal{W}_z,\ldots &\text{constants};\\
\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of
arity one};\\
\boldsymbol{\lambda} x,\boldsymbol{\lambda} y,\boldsymbol{\lambda}
z,\ldots
& \text{functional symbols of arity one};\\
\cdot\,,\,\circ & \text{functional symbols of arity two};\\
\langle -\,,\, -/ x\rangle,\langle -\,,\, -/ y\rangle,\langle -\,,\, -/ z\rangle,\ldots &
\text{functional symbols of arity two}.
\end{array}
$ \\[5pt]
 We
will omit $\cdot$, which denotes application. The sets of ground
terms and ground substitutions of $R$ are defined inductively as
follows:
\begin{align*}
M,N::&= a \mid  MN \mid \lambda a. M \mid\boldsymbol{\lambda} a. M\mid s\circ M \\
s,q::&= id \mid \mathcal{W}_{a} \mid \langle s\,,\,  N/ a \rangle \mid
s\circ q
\end{align*}
\end{definition}
 We will use the same abbreviations as in
Convention~\ref{notation2} and Convention~\ref{notation1}.
\newpage
\begin{definition}(The rewriting system $R$).\\[5pt]
$
\begin{array}{lll}
(Abs1) & s\circ \lambda a.M\rightarrow\lambda a.\langle
\mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs2) & s\circ \boldsymbol{\lambda}
a.M\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\lambda} a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\,
a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs3) & s\circ \lambda a.M\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\lambda}
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(Abs4) & s\circ \boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M\rightarrow\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/
a\rangle\circ M &\\
(App) & s\circ  MN\rightarrow(s\circ  M)(s\circ  N) &\\
(ConsVar) & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ a\rightarrow N &\\
(New) & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ b\rightarrow  s\circ b & (a\neq b)\\
(IdVar) &  id\circ a\rightarrow a &\\
(Clos) & s\circ q\circ M\rightarrow (s\circ q)\circ M &\\
(Ass) & s\circ q\circ  r\rightarrow (s\circ q)\circ r &\\
(IdR) & s\circ id\rightarrow s &\\
(IdShift) & id\circ \mathcal{W}_{a}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}_{a} &\\
(ConsShift) & \langle s\,,\, N/ a\rangle\circ \mathcal{W}_{a}\rightarrow s &\\
(Map) & s\circ \langle q\,,\, N/ a\rangle\rightarrow\langle
s\circ q \,,\, s\circ N/ a\rangle &\\
(\mathcal{W}_1) & \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ b\rightarrow b & (a\neq b)\\
(\mathcal{W}_2) & (s\circ\mathcal{W}_{a})\circ b\rightarrow s\circ b & (a \neq
b)\\
(\alpha) & \boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M\rightarrow\lambda
b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\, b/ a\rangle\circ M &\\
(\xi) & \boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M\rightarrow\lambda a.M &
\end{array}
$
\end{definition}
\begin{definition} To each term $M$  we assign
$FV(M)$ as in Definition~\ref{FV} with the additional case: \\
$\begin{array}{l} FV(\boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M)=FV(\lambda
a.M)=O_{\lambda a}(FV(M)) \end{array}$
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}Suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$ M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow M_n\rightarrow\ldots$$
 I claim that we can get
some
infinite  $R$-sequence\\
$$(M_1)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_2)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_n)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots$$
The proof is by induction over $n$. If $n$ is equal to $1$, there is nothing to prove. Else there are three cases.\\[5pt]
1)  If the reduction step $ M_n\rightarrow M_{n+1}$ is not
$Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\\ $R$-reduction of the
same name $(M_n)^*\rightarrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several
$\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2$ can
decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some
black lambda, this lambda may
turn pale. See Example~\ref{example1.18}.\\[5pt]
2) If  $M_n\rightarrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$,
we can apply $\alpha$:\\
$(M_n)^*\rightarrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~\ref{restriction}
and
Example~\ref{example1.13}).\\[5pt]
3) If $ M_n\rightarrow_{Abs} M_{n+1}$ and the $Abs$-redex is
$s\circ\lambda a.M$, there are four
possible subcases:\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
Subcase \,1. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin
FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 2. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 3. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase \,4. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);
\end{array}\\[3pt]
$ and we can apply $Abs_1, Abs_2, Abs_3$, and $Abs_4$,
respectively. See Examples~\ref{example1.14}, \ref{example1.15},
\ref{example1.16}, and \ref{example1.17}.

The proof is similar for substitutions. For judgements, suppose we
have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\Gamma_1\vdash M_1\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_2\vdash  M_2\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_3\vdash M_3\rightsquigarrow\ldots$$
We can obtain the $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence of terms
$$\Lambda\Gamma_1.M_1\arrow\arrow\Lambda\Gamma_2.M_2\arrow\arrow\Lambda\Gamma_3.M_3\arrow\arrow\ldots$$
where $\alpha_2$-steps are replaced by $\alpha_1$ and $Abs$.
\end{proof}
\begin{example}\label{example1.18}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\lambda x.\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ x\rangle\circ y\rightarrow_{New}\lambda
x.id\circ y\rightarrow\ldots$$
 becomes the following $R$-sequence
$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ x\rangle\circ
y\rightarrow_{New} \boldsymbol{\lambda} x.id\circ y \rightarrow_{\xi}\lambda
x.id\circ y\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.13}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
 $$\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ
 x\rightarrow_{\alpha_1}\lambda y.\langle\mathcal{W}_y\,,\, y/
 x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
  becomes the following  $R$-sequence
 $$\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow_{\alpha}\lambda y.\langle\mathcal{W}_y\,,\, y/
 x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
 \end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.14}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$id\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\, x/
x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
 becomes the following  $R$-sequence
$$ id\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs1}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\, x/
x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.15}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$id\circ\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\,
x/ x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
 becomes the following
$R$-sequence
$$id\circ\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ
x\rightarrow_{Abs2}\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\, x/
x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.16}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\langle id\,,\, x/ y\rangle\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda
x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\, x/ y\rangle\,,\, x/ x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
becomes the following  $R$-sequence
$$\langle id\,,\, x/
y\rangle\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs3} \boldsymbol{\lambda}
x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\, x/ y\rangle\,,\, x/ x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.17}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\langle id\,,\,\lambda y.y/ x\rangle\circ\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ
x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\,\lambda y.y/ x\rangle\,,\,
x/ x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
 becomes the following
$R$-sequence
$$\langle id\,,\,\lambda y.y/ x\rangle\circ\boldsymbol{\lambda}
x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow_{Abs4}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\,\lambda
y.y/ x\rangle\,,\, x/ x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
To prove that $R$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground
terms and ground substitutions, we use the method of semantic
labelling. See~\cite{Zantema}.
\begin{definition}
To each term $M$ and each substitution $s$ we put in correspondence  natural numbers  $|M|$ and $|s|$ respectively defined as follows:\\
$\begin{array}{l}
|\lambda a.M|=|M|+1\\
|\boldsymbol{\lambda} a.M|=|M|+1\\
|s\circ M|=|s|+|M|\\
|s\circ
q|=|s|+|q|\\
|MN|=max(|M|,|N|)\\
|\langle s\,,\, N/
a\rangle|=max(|s|,|N|)\\
|id|=0\\
|\mathcal{W}_{a}|=0\\
 |a|=0
 \end{array}$
\end{definition}
Note that any functional symbol of $R$ now turns to some
 monotone function of $\mathbb{N}$ to
$\mathbb{N}$ or of $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$.
Consider  the following two-sorted term rewriting system $Q$.
\begin{definition} The
signature
of $Q$ contains:\\
$
\begin{array}{ll}

\begin{proof}The proof is by induction over the structure of $M$. Let us consider four cases.\\[5pt]
Case 1: $M$ is a variable. The proof is trivial.\\[5pt]
 Case 2:  $ M$
has the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. By Generation
lemma, $\Gamma\vdash M$
has the form\\
$\Delta\,,\,b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\, a_1\vdash
(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$  \\
and we can apply $\alpha_2$ , because\\
 $FV(b\,,\,a_m\,,\,\ldots\,,\,
a_1\vdash (\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b)=\langle\{b\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle$\\[10pt]
 Case 3: $M$ has the form $\lambda a.N$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma,a\vdash
N$ is derivable. Suppose $N$ contains a block of the form
 $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. By
induction hypothesis, we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to
$\Gamma,a\vdash N$. But any application  of $\alpha_1$ or
$\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma,a\vdash N$ corresponds to some application
of $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ (and, in some cases, $Abs$) to
$\Gamma\vdash\lambda a.N$. For example,\\
$\Gamma,a\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_2}\Gamma,b \vdash\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ N$\\
corresponds to\\
 $\Gamma\vdash\lambda
a.N\rightsquigarrow_{\alpha_1}\Gamma\vdash\lambda b.\langle\mathcal{W}_{b}\,,\,
b/ a\rangle\circ N$\\[10pt]
 Case 4: $M$ has the form $NL$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma\vdash N$ and
$\Gamma\vdash L$ are derivable. Suppose one of these terms
contains a block of the form $(\mathcal{W}_{a_1\ldotsa_mb})\circ b$. For
clarity, let it be $N$. By induction hypothesis,  we can apply
$\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash N$. I claim that we can
apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash NL$. For the case
$\alpha_1$ is nothing to prove, because any $\alpha_1$-redex in
$N$ occurs in $NL$ too. For the case $\alpha_2$, suppose that
$\Gamma\vdash NL$ has the form $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$. Recall
that $FV(NL)=FV(N)\cup FV(L)$, hence $FV(N)\subseteq FV(NL)$. By
Lemma~\ref{monotone},\\ $FV(a,\Delta\vdash N))\subseteq FV(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$.\\
Hence if $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash N)$,
then $a\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(a,\Delta\vdash NL)$. If
we can apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash N$, then we can
apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,a,\Delta\vdash NL$.
\end{proof}
 Warning!
In general, the terms $N_1,\ldots,N_k$ in the statement of
Theorem~\ref{Subnf} are not pure.  For example, the judgement\\
$x,x\vdash\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ y\rangle\triangleright x,x,y$\\ is derivable
and the substitution\\ $\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ y\rangle$\\ is a
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form.

L$.  If this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise, suppose this sequence has the form
\\
$\Gamma\vdash M\rightsquigarrow\ldots\rightsquigarrow\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$,\\
where
$(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}  W$ and  $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}\sigma(W)$.\\
If the reduction step $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\vdash L$ belongs to
$\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$, everything is all right, because
$\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case. Indeed, $\Gamma\vdash M$
is derivable by Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Delta\vdash N$ and
$\Sigma\vdash L$ are derivable by Subject
reduction. Take any $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-normal form of $\Sigma\vdash L$ (this normal form exists by Theorem ~\ref{SN} and are derivable too) and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to get $ W\overset{\sigma}{\arrow\arrow}\sigma(V)$.\\
If $\Delta\vdash N\rightsquigarrow_{Beta}\Sigma\vdash L$, then
$W\rightarrow_{Beta}V$, because any $Beta$-redex in $N$ corresponds to
some $Beta$-redex in $W$, hence
$\sigma(W)\rightarrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}Suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$ M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow M_n\rightarrow\ldots$$
 I claim that we can get
some
infinite  $R$-sequence\\
$$(M_1)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_2)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}(M_n)^*\overset{R}{\arrow\arrow}\ldots$$
The proof is by induction over $n$. If $n$ is equal to $1$, there is nothing to prove. Else there are three cases.\\[5pt]
1)  If the reduction step $ M_n\rightarrow M_{n+1}$ is not
$Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\\ $R$-reduction of the
same name $(M_n)^*\rightarrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several
$\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\mathcal{W}_1,\mathcal{W}_2$ can
decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some
black lambda, this lambda may
turn pale. See Example~\ref{example1.18}.\\[5pt]
2) If  $M_n\rightarrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$,
we can apply $\alpha$:\\
$(M_n)^*\rightarrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~\ref{restriction}
and
Example~\ref{example1.13}).\\[5pt]
3) If $ M_n\rightarrow_{Abs} M_{n+1}$ and the $Abs$-redex is
$s\circ\lambda a.M$, there are four
possible subcases:\\
$
\begin{array}{lll}
Subcase \,1. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin
FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 2. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase\, 3. & a\notin FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\in FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);\\
Subcase \,4. & a\in FV_1(\lambda a.M),\, a\notin FV_1(\lambda
a.\langle \mathcal{W}_{a}\circ s\,,\, a/ a\rangle\circ M);
\end{array}\\[3pt]
$ and we can apply $Abs_1, Abs_2, Abs_3$, and $Abs_4$,
respectively. See Examples~\ref{example1.14}, \ref{example1.15},
\ref{example1.16}, and \ref{example1.17}.

The proof is similar for substitutions. For judgements, suppose we
have some infinite $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\Gamma_1\vdash M_1\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_2\vdash  M_2\rightsquigarrow\Gamma_3\vdash M_3\rightsquigarrow\ldots$$
We can obtain the $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence of terms
$$\Lambda\Gamma_1.M_1\arrow\arrow\Lambda\Gamma_2.M_2\arrow\arrow\Lambda\Gamma_3.M_3\arrow\arrow\ldots$$
where $\alpha_2$-steps are replaced by $\alpha_1$ and $Abs$.
\end{proof}

$$\lambda x.\langle id\,,\,\mathcal{W}_x\circ x/ x\rangle\circ y\rightarrow_{New}\lambda
x.id\circ y\rightarrow\ldots$$

y\rightarrow_{New} \boldsymbol{\lambda} x.id\circ y \rightarrow_{\xi}\lambda
x.id\circ y\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.13}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
 $$\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ

 x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
  becomes the following  $R$-sequence
 $$\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow_{\alpha}\lambda y.\langle\mathcal{W}_y\,,\, y/
 x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
 \end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.14}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$id\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\, x/
x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
 becomes the following  $R$-sequence
$$ id\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs1}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\, x/
x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.15}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$id\circ\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\,
x/ x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$

$R$-sequence
$$id\circ\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ
x\rightarrow_{Abs2}\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ id\,,\, x/
x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}
\begin{example}\label{example1.16}The $\sigma\mathcal{W}\alpha$-sequence
$$\langle id\,,\, x/ y\rangle\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda
x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\, x/ y\rangle\,,\, x/ x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
becomes the following  $R$-sequence
$$\langle id\,,\, x/
y\rangle\circ\lambda x.x\rightarrow_{Abs3} \boldsymbol{\lambda}
x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\, x/ y\rangle\,,\, x/ x\rangle\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$

$$\langle id\,,\,\lambda y.y/ x\rangle\circ\lambda x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ
x\rightarrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\,\lambda y.y/ x\rangle\,,\,
x/ x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$

$R$-sequence

x.\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow_{Abs4}\lambda x.\langle\mathcal{W}_x\circ\langle id\,,\,\lambda
y.y/ x\rangle\,,\, x/ x\rangle\circ\mathcal{W}_x\circ x\rightarrow\ldots$$
\end{example}

\begin{proof}
For any infinite $R$-sequence
$$M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow M_3\rightarrow\ldots$$
we can get some infinite $Q$-sequence simply by labelling all
symbols $\circ$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda} a$ by theirs own
values. See~\cite{Zantema}, Theorem~81 for details (see
also~\cite{Zantema}, Example~33). The proof  is similar for
substitutions.
\end{proof}

items.raw:
There is a gap between lambda calculi with explicit substitutions
using De Brujn indices and lambda calculi with explicit
substitutions using ordinary (named) variables. The first follow
 the spirit of category theory. The second attempt to reflect
the ``real way to work with bound variables". We clarify this with
an example. Simultaneous substitution  will be denoted by
$$[x_1/N_1\,,\, x_2/N_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, x_k/N_k]$$ Let's call this substitution $s$.
Suppose the variable $x$ is different from all
$x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k$. By $[s\,,\, x/N]$ denote the substitution
 $$[x_1/N_1\,,\, x_2/N_2\,,\,\ldots\,,\, x_k/N_k\,,\, x/N]$$
According
 to~\cite{Stoughton},
the substitution $s$ moves under a binder this way
$$(\lambda x.M)[s]\rightarrow\lambda y.(M[s\,,\, x/y])$$
where $y$ is a ``fresh" variable.  The similar reduction for
categorical combinators is
$$\Lambda( M)\circ s\rightarrow\Lambda(M\circ\langle s\circ F\,,\, S\rangle)$$
where $F$ denotes the first projection and $S$ denotes the second
projection. A significant difference is that in the latter case
the substitution $s$ is multiplied by the first projection. Abadi,
Cardelli, Curien, and Levy in \cite{Abadi} suggested to use the
substitution $\uparrow$, corresponding to the first projection,
together with named variables. They have obtained the equality
$$(\lambda x.M)[s]=\lambda x.(M[(x/
x)\cdot(s\,\circ\!\uparrow)])$$ We  rewrite this equality as
$$(\lambda x.M)[s]\rightarrow\lambda x.(M[s\,\circ\!\uparrow\,,\, x/
x])$$ Abadi, Cardelli, Curien, and Levy write ``In this notation,
intuitively,\\ $x[\uparrow]$ refers to $x$ after the first
binder." To clarify this point, consider some typed calculus with
contexts, where  contexts are finite lists of the form $x_1:A_1,
x_2:A_2,\ldots, x_k:A_k$, where $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_k$ are types and
\emph{repetitions of variables are permitted.}  A judgement of the
form $\Gamma\vdash x:A$ means ``the rightmost occurrences of the
variable $x$ in the context $\Gamma$ has type $A$." For example,
the judgement $x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash x:B$ is true, but the judgement
$x:A\,,\, x:B\vdash x:A$ is not true. But the judgement $x:A\,,\,
x:B\vdash x[\uparrow]:A$ is true.  The crucial idea is this: if we
allow repetitions of identical variables as in $\lambda x.\lambda
x.M$, then we must allow repetitions in contexts too. In this way
we will obtain some lambda calculus with explicit
substitutions and named variables such that:\\
 (1) It is close to  the calculi of categorical combinators;\\
 (2) It is convenient to work;\\
 (3) Renaming of bound variables when
performing substitutions is done using  special reductions and may
be delayed.
